title: DNS: Names, Records & Resolvers
sub: Resolve names with dig, nslookup, host and the macOS resolver, read every record type, and spot DNS problems fast
goals: Explain the path of a lookup from the stub resolver to an authoritative server
Read all sections of a dig answer, including flags, status and TTL
Query a specific resolver or an authoritative server directly and compare answers
Predict which macOS tools honour /etc/hosts, search domains and per-domain resolvers
Build dnscheck, a script that reports A, MX, NS and TXT records and compares public resolvers

blocks.text: Almost every connection starts with a question: what address belongs to this name? The Domain Name System answers it, and when it fails, everything looks broken even though the network is fine. Many outages that get described as "the internet is down" are DNS failures: `ping 1.1.1.1` works, `ping example.com` does not. In this chapter you will learn how a lookup travels, which tool sees which part of the macOS resolver, how to read a `dig` answer line by line, and how to build `dnscheck`, a small tool that tells you what the world sees for a domain.

blocks.title: Ask about domains, do not attack them

blocks.text: Looking up public records with `dig` is normal and harmless. Do not run zone transfers (`dig AXFR`) or bulk-guess subdomains against domains you do not own. Use `example.com`, `iana.org`, your own domains, and the lab. Public resolvers such as `1.1.1.1`, `8.8.8.8` and `9.9.9.9` are fine for a few queries; do not hammer them in a tight loop.
How a lookup travels
Four kinds of machine take part in resolving `www.example.com`.

blocks.code:
stub resolver          recursive resolver        root        com. TLD     example.com
  (in your Mac)          (router/ISP/1.1.1.1)      servers     servers      authoritative
       │ 1. www.example.com A?  │                    │            │             │
       │ ─────────────────────▶ │ 2. who runs com?   │            │             │
       │                        │ ──────────────────▶│            │             │
       │                        │ ◀ ask a.gtld-servers.net        │             │
       │                        │ 3. who runs example.com?        │             │
       │                        │ ───────────────────────────────▶│             │
       │                        │ ◀ ask a.iana-servers.net        │             │
       │                        │ 4. www.example.com A?                         │
       │                        │ ─────────────────────────────────────────────▶│
       │                        │ ◀ 93.184.216.34, TTL 300                      │
       │ 5. answer + TTL        │ (now cached for 300 s)                        │
       │ ◀───────────────────── │                                               │

items.text: The **stub resolver** is the small client library inside your Mac. It does no research. It asks a configured recursive resolver and waits. On macOS the stub is part of `mDNSResponder`, which also handles `.local` names and keeps a cache.

The **recursive resolver** does the research for you. If it has the answer cached, it replies at once. If not, it asks the **root servers** who runs `com.`, asks a `com.` server who runs `example.com`, then asks the **authoritative** server, the one that holds the actual records. It caches everything it learns.
**Authoritative servers** own a zone. They give a final answer (flag `aa`) or a **referral** pointing deeper.

Every record carries a **TTL** (time to live, in seconds): how long a cache may keep it. A TTL of 300 means a change you publish reaches everyone within about five minutes at worst; 86400 means up to a day.

blocks.text: A name is read right to left. `www.example.com.` has a hidden trailing dot for the root, then the **TLD** `com`, then the **domain** `example`, then the **host label** `www`. Each dot is a potential **delegation**: the parent zone holds NS records saying "for names below here, ask these servers".

blocks.title: Why caching decides what you see

blocks.text: Because answers are cached at the stub, at the recursive resolver and often inside the application, two machines on the same network can see different answers for minutes after a change. This is why DNS changes "take time to propagate": nothing travels. Old copies simply expire at different moments.
Which tool sees which part

macOS does not use `/etc/resolv.conf` for normal lookups. Resolver settings live in the System Configuration database, which can hold **several resolvers at once**, each limited to certain domains or interfaces. You saw `scutil --dns` in [See your own network](#net-local). The consequence is that macOS command-line tools split into two families.

head: Path
Tools
What they use
rows: `/etc/hosts`, search domains, `.local` multicast DNS, per-domain resolvers in `/etc/resolver/`, VPN resolvers, the cache

Only the nameserver(s) in `/etc/resolv.conf` (generated from the primary resolver), or the one you name with `@server`. No hosts file, no search domains by default, no `.local` multicast, no per-domain routing

blocks.text: This is the single most useful fact in the chapter. **If `dig` and `ping` disagree, they took different paths.** `dig intranet.corp.example` may fail because it asked your home router, while `ping intranet.corp.example` succeeds because the system resolver sent that domain to the VPN's DNS server.
Resolver configuration in `scutil --dns`

blocks.code:
$ scutil --dns | head -40
DNS configuration

resolver #1
  search domain[0] : lan
  nameserver[0] : 192.168.1.1
  if_index : 14 (en0)
  flags    : Request A records
  reach    : 0x00020002 (Reachable,Directly Reachable Address)

resolver #2
  domain   : local
  options  : mdns
  timeout  : 5
  flags    : Request A records
  order    : 300000

resolver #3
  domain   : corp.example
  nameserver[0] : 10.8.0.1
  if_index : 16 (utun4)
  flags    : Request A records
  reach    : 0x00000002 (Reachable)
  order    : 100000

items.text: **resolver #1** is the default: names that match nothing more specific go to `192.168.1.1`. Its **search domain** `lan` means a short name is retried with `.lan` appended, so `ping pi` can find `pi.lan`.

**resolver #2** says names ending in `.local` are resolved by **multicast DNS (mDNS, Bonjour)**: the Mac asks the whole link at `224.0.0.251` port 5353 and the owning device answers. That is how `macbook.local` resolves without any server.

**resolver #3** is **split DNS**: names under `corp.example` go to `10.8.0.1` through the VPN tunnel, and nothing else does. Ordinary lookups still use your home resolver, so they stay fast and private.

blocks.text: Administrators and tools add their own per-domain resolvers by creating a file named after the domain in `/etc/resolver/`, containing `nameserver 10.1.0.53`. Local development setups use this to send `.test` names to a local DNS server such as `dnsmasq`. See `man 5 resolver`.
Encrypted DNS and DNSSEC in brief

Classic DNS travels in plain text over UDP port 53 (and TCP 53 for large answers), so your network can see and alter every lookup. **DNS over HTTPS (DoH)** and **DNS over TLS (DoT)** wrap the same questions in encryption. macOS supports them through DNS settings profiles, and browsers such as Firefox and Chrome can do their own DoH, bypassing the system resolver and local rules like a hosts file or a Pi-hole style sinkhole. When one browser resolves something differently from `ping`, check whether it has its own secure DNS setting.

**DNSSEC** is a different protection: authoritative zones sign their records, and a validating resolver checks the signatures. It proves an answer is genuine, not that the query was private. A validating resolver sets the `ad` (authenticated data) flag in its reply; `dig +dnssec` shows the signatures.
Record types
A DNS zone is a set of **resource records**. Each has an owner name, a TTL, a class (`IN`, for Internet), a type and data. The type says what the data means.

head: Type
Meaning
Example data
rows: Alias: this name is another name; resolve that one instead
Mail exchanger with a preference number (lower is tried first)
Authoritative name server for the zone
Free text: SPF, DKIM, DMARC, domain verification
Start of authority: primary server, admin mailbox, serial, refresh/retry/expire, negative TTL
Reverse mapping from an address back to a name, under `in-addr.arpa`
Service location: priority, weight, port, target
Which certificate authorities may issue certificates for the domain

blocks.text: Samples in this book, and the practice terminal, use `93.184.216.34`, the long-standing address of `example.com`. That domain has since moved to a different provider and returns several addresses that can change, so `dig example.com` on your Mac shows other numbers. The records, TTLs and lookup steps work the same way.
Rules that cause real trouble:

items.text: A name that has a **CNAME** cannot have other records at the same name (so you cannot put a CNAME at the bare domain `example.com`, which must have SOA and NS).
**MX** and **NS** records point at *names*, never at addresses or CNAMEs. A mail server needs its own A or AAAA record.
A **null MX** (`0 .`) states that a domain accepts no mail at all.

**PTR** records live in the reverse zone, controlled by whoever owns the *address block* (usually your ISP or cloud provider), not by the owner of the domain. IPv4 reverse names list the octets backwards: `93.184.216.34` becomes `34.216.184.93.in-addr.arpa`. IPv6 uses `ip6.arpa` with one label per hex digit.
**TXT** records for mail authentication are strings that begin `v=spf1`, `v=DKIM1` or `v=DMARC1`, and are published at the names `domain`, `selector._domainkey.domain` and `_dmarc.domain`.

blocks.text: dig: the tool for reading DNS

`dig` (domain information groper) is a DNS client that prints the raw reply. Its output looks cluttered at first, but every line has a fixed meaning. Here is a full answer from the practice terminal, which you can reproduce for any name.

blocks.code:
$ dig example.com

; <<>> DiG 9.10.6 <<>> example.com
;; global options: +cmd
;; Got answer:
;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: NOERROR, id: 41872
;; flags: qr rd ra; QUERY: 1, ANSWER: 1, AUTHORITY: 0, ADDITIONAL: 1

;; OPT PSEUDOSECTION:
; EDNS: version: 0, flags:; udp: 1232
;; QUESTION SECTION:
;example.com.			IN	A

;; ANSWER SECTION:
example.com.		300	IN	A	93.184.216.34

;; Query time: 14 msec
;; SERVER: 192.168.1.1#53(192.168.1.1)
;; WHEN: Thu Oct 08 09:41:00 BST 2026
;; MSG SIZE  rcvd: 76

head: Part of the reply
What it tells you
rows: Banner: the dig version and your command line
The result code. `NOERROR` means the query worked, `NXDOMAIN` the name does not exist, `SERVFAIL` the resolver could not get an answer, `REFUSED` it will not answer you
`qr` is a response, `rd` recursion was desired, `ra` the server offers it. `aa` would mean authoritative, `ad` DNSSEC-validated, `tc` truncated (retry over TCP)
How many records each section holds
What was asked: name, class `IN`, type `A`
The records that answer it: name, TTL in seconds, class, type, data
How long this server took to answer
Which resolver actually answered, and the port

blocks.title: Asking one specific resolver for one record type

tokens.exp: ask this resolver instead of the system default

blocks.text: Two more sections appear when relevant. **AUTHORITY** lists the name servers responsible for the zone (in referrals and for negative answers, where it carries the SOA that sets how long the "no such name" is cached). **ADDITIONAL** carries helpful extras, such as the addresses of those servers (glue).

Everyday work uses `dig` in short forms. `+short` prints only the data. `+noall +answer` hides everything except the answer section, keeping the TTL and record type, which makes the output easy to parse.

blocks.name: dig
blocks.sum: Send a DNS query to a chosen resolver and print the full, structured reply.

how.text: `dig` builds a DNS query for a name and record type (A by default), sends it over UDP to a server, and prints the response sections. Unlike `ping` or `curl`, it does not use the macOS system resolver: it reads the first nameserver from `/etc/resolv.conf`, or the server you name with `@server`. That makes it the right tool to ask "what does *this* resolver say?" and the wrong one to ask "what would my apps see?".

Options starting with `+` change query behaviour and output, `-x` builds a reverse lookup, and `@server` chooses the target. Order among name, type, `@server` and `+options` is free. Recursion is on by default (`+recurse`); `+norecurse` asks a server only for what it knows, which is how you query an authoritative server without it going off to research.

flags.d: Query this resolver or name server instead of the default.
Print only the record data, one answer per line.
Turn off all sections, then turn on just the answer section: name, TTL, class, type, data.
Start at the root and follow the delegations yourself, printing each referral.
Show or hide the final statistics block (query time, server, size).
Reverse lookup: build the `in-addr.arpa` (or `ip6.arpa`) name for you.
Use TCP instead of UDP; useful when a reply is truncated or UDP is blocked.
Ask for DNSSEC records (RRSIG) and show the `ad` flag if the resolver validated.
Do not ask the server to research; it answers from its own data only.
Per-try timeout in seconds, and number of tries. Use `+time=2 +tries=1` in scripts so dead servers do not stall them.
Omit the leading banner lines.
Batch mode: run one query per line of a file, each line holding dig arguments such as a name or `example.com MX`.
Force IPv4 or IPv6 transport.

gotchas: `dig +short` on an alias prints the **CNAME target first**, then the addresses. To get only IPs, filter with `grep -E '^[0-9.]+$'` or ask for the final answer with `awk`.
`dig` does not read `/etc/hosts` and does not append search domains (`+nosearch` is the default). A short name like `pi` returns nothing even though `ping pi` works.

A reply that never comes ends with `;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached`. That is a network or firewall problem, not a missing name. A missing name is a quick reply with status NXDOMAIN.
notes: At the time of writing macOS ships ISC `dig` 9.10.6 (check with `dig -v`). `brew install bind` provides a current build, which prints a few extra lines such as COOKIE but is used the same way.

blocks.text: Status values and flags you will actually meet

head: Status or flag
Meaning
What to do
rows: The name exists but has no record of the type you asked
Try another type, such as AAAA or CNAME
Check spelling, check the zone, check which resolver you asked
The resolver tried and failed: broken delegation, unreachable authoritative servers, DNSSEC validation failure
Ask another resolver; query the authoritative server directly
The server declines to answer you
You asked a server that does not offer recursion or has an access list
The answer came from an authoritative server
You are looking at the source of truth
Missing `ra` means you queried an authoritative-only server
Truncated; the full answer did not fit in UDP
Only trust it from a resolver you trust

blocks.text: Watching the cache count down
Ask a caching resolver for the same record twice and look at the TTL. It counts down, because you are seeing the resolver's cached copy and its remaining life.

blocks.code:
$ dig +noall +answer @1.1.1.1 example.com
example.com.		219	IN	A	93.184.216.34
$ sleep 30; dig +noall +answer @1.1.1.1 example.com
example.com.		189	IN	A	93.184.216.34
$ dig +noall +answer @a.iana-servers.net. example.com
example.com.		300	IN	A	93.184.216.34

blocks.text: The cached copy shows the remaining life (219, then 189). The authoritative server always reports the full configured TTL, because it owns the record rather than a copy. Seeing a TTL lower than the zone's value is how you recognise a cached answer. Large providers run many caches behind one address, so successive queries sometimes show jumping TTLs.
+trace: do the resolver's job by hand

`dig +trace` starts at the root and follows each referral itself, without using any cache. It shows exactly who delegates to whom, which makes it the right tool for "the domain works on some resolvers but not others".

blocks.code:
$ dig +trace example.com
; <<>> DiG 9.10.6 <<>> +trace example.com
;; global options: +cmd
.			518400	IN	NS	a.root-servers.net.
.			518400	IN	NS	b.root-servers.net.
...
;; Received 811 bytes from 192.168.1.1#53(192.168.1.1) in 21 ms

com.			172800	IN	NS	a.gtld-servers.net.
com.			172800	IN	NS	b.gtld-servers.net.
...
;; Received 1173 bytes from 198.41.0.4#53(a.root-servers.net) in 24 ms

example.com.		172800	IN	NS	a.iana-servers.net.
example.com.		172800	IN	NS	b.iana-servers.net.
;; Received 187 bytes from 192.5.6.30#53(a.gtld-servers.net) in 31 ms

example.com.		300	IN	A	93.184.216.34
;; Received 56 bytes from 199.43.135.53#53(a.iana-servers.net) in 88 ms

blocks.text: Each block is one hop of the chain you drew earlier: your resolver's list of root servers, the root's referral to `com.`, the `com.` servers' referral to `example.com`, and finally the authoritative answer. If a trace stops with `SERVFAIL` or no answer at one step, the break is in that delegation.
The other DNS tools

`nslookup`, `host` and `whois` ship with macOS and are simpler than `dig`. Like `dig`, `nslookup` and `host` talk to DNS servers directly. The two native macOS tools, `dscacheutil` and `dns-sd`, go through the system's own machinery.

blocks.name: nslookup
blocks.sum: A simple DNS lookup client with a plain, human-oriented output and an interactive mode.

how.text: `nslookup` asks a DNS server for a name and prints the server it used and the answer. By default it labels the reply "Non-authoritative answer" when it came from a cache. Run with no arguments it starts an interactive prompt where `set type=MX` changes the record type and `server 1.1.1.1` changes the resolver; press Ctrl-D to leave. Like `dig`, it uses DNS only, not the hosts file.

Optional last argument: ask this DNS server.

gotchas: The first `Address:` line is the **server's** (with `#53`), the later ones are the answer. A pattern like `^Address: ` (with the space) skips the server line, which prints `Address:<tab>`.

blocks.name: host
blocks.sum: Print DNS answers as short English sentences; the quickest way to see A, AAAA and MX together.

how.text: `host` queries A, AAAA and MX records by default and prints one sentence per record, so a single command shows how a name is reachable and where its mail goes. With an IP address instead of a name it performs the reverse lookup automatically. It uses DNS only.

blocks.name: whois
blocks.sum: Look up registration data for a domain or an IP block: registrar, dates, name servers, owner contact when public.

how.text: `whois` is a separate, much older protocol (TCP port 43) than DNS. It queries a registry or regional internet registry for who registered a domain or who owns an address block. Many registries now redact personal contact details. The record often contains the **registrar**, the **creation and expiry dates** and the **name servers**, which are useful evidence when a domain stops resolving because it expired.

flags.d: Ask a specific whois server instead of letting `whois` choose.

examples.desc: When does a domain expire?
Pull out the dates
Which network owns an address?

gotchas: Field names differ between registries (`Registry Expiry Date`, `Expiration Date`, `paid-till`), so grep case-insensitively with alternations.

blocks.name: dscacheutil
blocks.sum: Look up a name through the macOS system resolver, and manage its cache.
blocks.syntax: dscacheutil -q host -a name hostname | -q host -a ip_address addr | -flushcache | -cachedump | -statistics

how.text: `dscacheutil` talks to the Directory Services cache that fronts the system resolver. `-q host -a name HOST` is the one lookup tool that behaves exactly like an application: it honours `/etc/hosts`, search domains, mDNS and per-domain resolvers. If `dig` says the name resolves and `dscacheutil -q host` does not (or the other way round), you have found the difference between "DNS" and "what my apps see".
`-flushcache` discards the cached entries. On current macOS that is only part of a full flush; see the next card.

blocks.name: dns-sd
blocks.sum: Browse and resolve Bonjour (multicast DNS) services and names on the local link.
blocks.syntax: dns-sd -B type domain | -L name type domain | -G v4|v6|v4v6 hostname | -q name [type]

how.text: `dns-sd` is the command-line client for DNS Service Discovery and multicast DNS. `-B` browses for instances of a service type on the local network (`_ssh._tcp`, `_airplay._tcp`, `_ipp._tcp` for printers), `-L` resolves one instance to a host and port, and `-G` resolves a `.local` name to addresses. The command keeps running and prints changes as devices appear and leave; press Ctrl-C to stop.

flags.d: Browse for services of a type, usually in domain `local`.
Look up one service instance: target host, port and TXT data.
Resolve a hostname to its addresses.
Query any record by name and type through mDNS.

examples.desc: Which machines offer SSH on this network?

gotchas: `dns-sd` never exits by itself. For scripts, wrap it in a timeout. macOS has no `timeout` command; `brew install coreutils` provides `gtimeout`. Instance names with spaces break the `$NF` trick, which keeps only the last word.

blocks.text: /etc/hosts: the oldest DNS
Before DNS, every machine had one file mapping names to addresses. It still exists, and the system resolver reads it **before asking any DNS server**.

blocks.name: /etc/hosts
blocks.sum: A local text file that maps names to addresses and overrides DNS for every program that uses the system resolver.
blocks.syntax: ADDRESS NAME [ALIAS ...]      # one mapping per line, # starts a comment

how.text: Each line is an address followed by one or more names, separated by spaces or tabs. The default file defines `localhost` for IPv4 and IPv6 and `broadcasthost`. Apps that call the system resolver (browsers, `curl`, `ping`, `ssh`) check this file first, so a line here wins over any DNS record. `dig`, `host` and `nslookup` do not read it.

The file is root-owned, so editing needs `sudo`. Changes normally apply immediately; if an app still shows the old address, flush the cache (next section). Common uses: pointing a development name at `127.0.0.1`, testing a site on a new server before changing DNS, and blocking a domain by mapping it to `0.0.0.0`.

Back it up before editing

the first name (use the reserved .test suffix for development)

gotchas: Use `.test`, `.example` or `.invalid` for fake names. Do not invent names under `.local`: that suffix is reserved for multicast DNS and behaves oddly and slowly.
A typo in this file is a quiet outage. Keep the backup. Malware also edits it to redirect banking sites, so an unexpected line is a red flag.
Browsers using their own DoH ignore the file entirely.

blocks.title: Back up before you edit system files

blocks.text: `sudo cp /etc/hosts /etc/hosts.bak` first. Edit with `sudo nano /etc/hosts` or append with `tee -a` as shown. Never use `>` instead of `>>` with `tee` or redirection on this file; it would erase the `localhost` lines and several system services depend on them. To restore: `sudo cp /etc/hosts.bak /etc/hosts`.

blocks.code:
$ echo "127.0.0.1 myapp.test" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts
127.0.0.1 myapp.test
$ ping -c 1 myapp.test
PING myapp.test (127.0.0.1): 56 data bytes
64 bytes from 127.0.0.1: icmp_seq=0 ttl=64 time=0.062 ms
$ dig +short myapp.test
$ dscacheutil -q host -a name myapp.test
name: myapp.test
ip_address: 127.0.0.1

blocks.text: `ping` and `dscacheutil` agree; `dig` prints nothing because it never looked at the file. That small experiment shows the two resolver families more clearly than any diagram.
Flushing the cache
Caches exist at several levels, and you can only clear the ones on your own machine.

head: Where
How to clear it
rows: restart the browser, or its internal page (`chrome://net-internals/#dns` in Chrome)
restart the router, or wait for the TTL
you cannot; wait for the TTL, or ask another resolver

blocks.name: flush DNS cache
blocks.sum: Clear the macOS resolver cache so the next lookup goes back to the network.

how.text: Current macOS releases keep resolver results in the `mDNSResponder` daemon. Telling it to reload with the HUP signal discards its cache. `dscacheutil -flushcache` clears the Directory Services layer in front of it. The pair has worked unchanged across recent macOS versions and is safe: nothing is lost except cached answers, which are rebuilt on demand.

examples.desc: Flush both layers

anat.exp: run the next command even if the first printed nothing
signal the resolver daemon to reload and drop its cache

examples.desc: Flush, then prove the next lookup is fresh by timing it
examples.code: sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder; dig {{domain}} | grep 'Query time'

gotchas: Flushing helps only when the stale answer lives on your Mac. If the router or ISP resolver caches an old record, flushing changes nothing. Compare with `dig @1.1.1.1` to tell the difference.
The commands print nothing on success. No output is the expected result.

blocks.text: On macOS 12 and later the pair above is the standard recipe. Very old releases used different commands (`discoveryutil`, `lookupd`). If you read a flush recipe with those names, it is out of date.
Pipe recipes
The sections above taught the vocabulary. These recipes are what you will actually run. They use `hosts.txt` from the lab (ten domains), and public resolvers.
**Resolve a list of names, one line each.** Filter the output of `dig +short` to the first IPv4 address, because an alias prints its CNAME name first.

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ for h in $(cat hosts.txt); do echo $h $(dig +short $h | head -1); done

python.org 151.101.0.223
github.com 140.82.121.3
wikipedia.org 185.15.58.224
cloudflare.com 104.16.132.229
mozilla.org 34.160.144.191
kernel.org 139.178.84.217
debian.org 151.101.194.132
openbsd.org 199.185.178.80
iana.org 192.0.43.8

blocks.text: Against the real internet, protect the loop from CNAME lines and slow servers:

blocks.code:
while read -r h; do
  ip=$(dig +short +time=2 +tries=1 "$h" A | grep -E '^[0-9.]+$' | head -1)
  print "$h ${ip:-NXDOMAIN-or-timeout}"
done < hosts.txt

blocks.title: Resolve every name in a file, safely

tokens.exp: loop: read one line into h, -r keeps backslashes literal
run dig with short output, 2 s per try, one try
keep only lines that look like IPv4 addresses, dropping CNAME names
print the name and the address, or a marker when empty
end of loop; feed the loop from the file

blocks.text: **Find the primary mail server of a domain.** MX data is `priority hostname`. Sort by the first column numerically and take the first row.

**Compare three public resolvers.** If your router's answer is different from all three, your router is rewriting DNS. If one resolver differs, suspect that resolver, a stale cache, or a CDN that gives different answers by location.

blocks.code:
for r in 1.1.1.1 8.8.8.8 9.9.9.9; do
  print "$r  $(dig +short +time=2 +tries=1 @$r {{domain}} A | sort | paste -sd' ' -)"
done

blocks.text: **Show TTLs.** Name, remaining TTL and data, aligned.
**Find the authoritative servers, then ask one directly.** Without recursion the server answers only from its own data, and the `aa` flag confirms it is the source of truth.

blocks.code:
ns=$(dig +short {{domain}} NS | head -1)
dig @$ns {{domain}} A +norecurse | grep -A1 -E 'flags:|ANSWER SECTION'

blocks.text: **Reverse-resolve every address in a file.** Most private and consumer addresses have no PTR record, so expect many blanks.

blocks.code:
sort -u ips.txt | while read -r ip; do
  name=$(dig -x $ip +short | head -1)
  print "$ip ${name:--}"
done

blocks.text: **Detect DNS rewriting.** The `.invalid` TLD can never exist (RFC 2606). A correct resolver returns nothing for it. A resolver that answers with an address is rewriting failures into ads or captive portals.
**Check which names fail.** Print the status code for each name in a list; anything other than `NOERROR` is worth a look.

blocks.code: while read -r h; do print "$h $(dig +time=2 +tries=1 "$h" | grep -o 'status: [A-Z]*' | cut -d' ' -f2)"; done < hosts.txt

blocks.text: `ping 1.1.1.1` works but `ping example.com` fails: DNS. `dig @1.1.1.1 example.com` works but `dig example.com` fails: your default resolver (usually the router) is the problem; try changing DNS servers, or check `scutil --dns`. `dig` works but `ping` fails: look at `/etc/hosts`, search domains and per-domain resolvers, or a VPN. `dig` and `ping` both work but one app does not: the app has its own DNS settings (DoH) or proxy.
Common mistakes

items.text: **Trusting `dig` to predict what apps do.** Use `dscacheutil -q host -a name` or `ping` for the system view.
**Reading CNAME lines as addresses.** `dig +short` on an alias prints the alias target first.
**Flushing and expecting the world to change.** You cleared your cache, not your router's or the ISP's.
**Confusing NXDOMAIN with a timeout.** NXDOMAIN is a fast, definite "no". A timeout means the query never got an answer.
**Setting DNS on the wrong service.** `networksetup -setdnsservers` takes a **service** name such as `Wi-Fi`, not `en0`.
**Using `.local` for home servers.** That suffix is for multicast DNS; use `.lan`, `.home.arpa` or a real domain.
**Editing records and testing immediately.** Remember the old TTL. Lower it a day before a planned change.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Resolve a whole list

task.text: For every name in `hosts.txt`, print the name and its first address on one line (`name ip`). In the practice terminal and on your Mac, the result should have exactly ten lines.

hints: `for h in $(cat hosts.txt); do ...; done` or `while read -r h`.
`dig +short name | head -1` returns the first line.
blocks.solution: for h in $(cat hosts.txt); do echo $h $(dig +short $h | head -1); done

why.text: `$( )` captures the address and `echo` prints it next to the name. On the real internet add `grep -E '^[0-9.]+$'` before `head -1` so an alias target is not mistaken for an address.

blocks.verify: [[ $(for h in $(cat hosts.txt); do echo $h $(dig +short $h | head -1); done | wc -l) -eq 10 ]] && echo OK

blocks.title: NXDOMAIN or timeout?

task.text: Run `dig nosuchname.example.com` and note the status. Then run `dig @192.0.2.1 example.com +time=2 +tries=1` (that address is documentation space, so nothing answers). Compare the two outputs and explain the difference in one sentence each.

hints: Look at the `status:` field in the first, and at the last lines of the second.

why.text: The first receives a prompt, definite reply with status NXDOMAIN: the resolver works, the name does not exist. The second prints `connection timed out; no servers could be reached`: no DNS server ever answered, so the problem is reachability, not the name.

blocks.title: Override a name and prove who ignores it

task.text: On your Mac, back up `/etc/hosts`, map `myapp.test` to `127.0.0.1`, and then run `ping -c 1 myapp.test`, `dig +short myapp.test` and `dscacheutil -q host -a name myapp.test`. Say which tools saw your line. Finally restore the file.

hints: Append with `echo ... | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts`; never use `>`.
blocks.solution:
sudo cp /etc/hosts /etc/hosts.bak
echo "127.0.0.1 myapp.test" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts
ping -c 1 myapp.test
dig +short myapp.test
dscacheutil -q host -a name myapp.test
sudo cp /etc/hosts.bak /etc/hosts

why.text: `ping` and `dscacheutil` use the system resolver, which reads the hosts file first, so they see the line. `dig` speaks DNS only and prints nothing. The backup and restore make the experiment fully reversible.

blocks.title: Primary mail server

task.text: Print only the hostname of the mail server with the lowest preference number for `gmail.com`. Then do the same for `example.com` and explain what you see.

hints: MX data is "priority hostname". Sort numerically on the first field.
blocks.solution:
dig +short gmail.com MX | sort -n | head -1 | awk '{print $2}'
dig +short example.com MX

why.text: The lowest preference value is tried first. At the time of writing `example.com` publishes a null MX (`0 .`), which states that the domain accepts no mail, so the hostname field is just a dot. If you see a real hostname there, the record has changed; the method is the same.

blocks.title: Resolver comparison

task.text: Ask `1.1.1.1`, `8.8.8.8` and `9.9.9.9` for the A record of `example.com`, printing one line per resolver with the sorted answers on that line. Then add the TTL from each resolver as a second column. Which TTLs differ, and why?

hints: `dig +short @$r name A` for the answers; `dig +noall +answer @$r name A | awk 'NR==1 {print $2}'` for the TTL.
blocks.solution:
for r in 1.1.1.1 8.8.8.8 9.9.9.9; do
  ttl=$(dig +noall +answer @$r example.com A | awk 'NR==1 {print $2}')
  ans=$(dig +short @$r example.com A | sort | paste -sd' ' -)
  print "$r ttl=$ttl $ans"
done

why.text: Each resolver has its own cache, so the remaining TTL differs, even though the data is identical. Different data would suggest one resolver is out of date, rewriting answers, or a CDN steering by location.

blocks.title: Why does dig fail but ping work?

task.text: A laptop is on a company VPN. `ping wiki.corp.example` works. `dig wiki.corp.example` returns `NXDOMAIN`. `scutil --dns` shows resolver #1 with `nameserver[0] : 192.168.1.1` and resolver #3 with `domain : corp.example` and `nameserver[0] : 10.8.0.1 (utun4)`.

items.text: Why do the two commands disagree?
How would you ask the same question as `ping` using a DNS tool?
Which command shows what applications see?

hints: Which resolver does `dig` read from, and which does the system resolver use for names under `corp.example`?
blocks.solution:
1. `ping` uses the system resolver, which sends `corp.example` names to the VPN's server at 10.8.0.1. `dig` reads only the default nameserver, the home router 192.168.1.1, which has never heard of the internal name and says NXDOMAIN.
2. `dig @10.8.0.1 wiki.corp.example +short`.
3. `dscacheutil -q host -a name wiki.corp.example` (or just `ping`).

why.text: macOS can hold several resolvers and routes each query by domain. `dig` bypasses that routing; the system resolver applies it. Always test with the tool that matches what the failing program does.

questions.why: `ping`, `curl`, `ssh` and other programs use the system resolver, which reads the hosts file first. `dig`, `nslookup` and `host` send DNS queries directly.

questions.q: In a dig reply, what does `status: NXDOMAIN` mean?
questions.why: NXDOMAIN is a definite answer: the queried name is not in the zone. A timeout produces no reply at all.

questions.q: You see a TTL of 189 from `dig @1.1.1.1 example.com`, but the zone's TTL is 300. What does that tell you?

options.text: You are looking at a cached copy with 189 seconds left

questions.why: Caches count a record's TTL down. The authoritative server returns the full configured value.

questions.q: Which command clears your Mac's DNS cache on current macOS?
questions.why: Telling `mDNSResponder` to reload with the HUP signal drops its cache; `dscacheutil -flushcache` clears the Directory Services layer. Both need `sudo`.

questions.q: Which record type holds a reverse mapping from an address to a name?
questions.why: PTR records live under `in-addr.arpa` (IPv4) or `ip6.arpa` (IPv6). `dig -x ADDRESS` builds the name for you.

questions.q: `dig +short www.example.net` prints a name first, then an IP. Why?

options.text: It is a bug in dig
www.example.net is a CNAME, and +short prints the alias target before the addresses
The name has two A records
The resolver is rewriting the answer

questions.why: A CNAME answer is followed by the records of its target, and `+short` prints each record's data in order. Filter with `grep -E '^[0-9.]+$'` for addresses only.

blocks.text: Build `dnscheck.zsh`: give it a domain and it reports the A, AAAA, MX, NS and TXT records, compares three public resolvers, asks an authoritative server directly, and tests whether your resolver rewrites failures. It is the tool you will run first when a name misbehaves, and `netdoctor` in [Troubleshooting](#troubleshoot) will call it.
Step 1: Helpers and the record report
A wrapper function gives every query sane timeouts. A second function prints a heading. Colours come from zsh's `print -P`.

blocks.code:
#!/bin/zsh
# dnscheck.zsh DOMAIN - what does DNS say about this name?
setopt pipefail
domain=${1:?usage: dnscheck.zsh DOMAIN}
resolvers=(1.1.1.1 8.8.8.8 9.9.9.9)

q()  { dig +short +time=2 +tries=1 "$@" }          # short answers with timeouts
hr() { print -P "%F{cyan}== $1 ==%f" }               # section heading

hr "Addresses"
print "A     $(q $domain A    | paste -sd' ' -)"
print "AAAA  $(q $domain AAAA | paste -sd' ' -)"

hr "Mail (best first)"
q $domain MX | sort -n

hr "Name servers"
q $domain NS | sort

hr "TXT"
q $domain TXT

blocks.text: Step 2: Compare the resolvers
Store each resolver's sorted answer in an associative array keyed by the answer text. If the array ends up with more than one key, the resolvers disagree.

blocks.code:
hr "Resolvers"
typeset -A seen
for r in $resolvers; do
  ans=$(q @$r $domain A | sort | paste -sd' ' -)
  printf '%-9s %s\n' $r "${ans:-NO ANSWER}"
  seen[${ans:-none}]=1
done
(( ${#seen} > 1 )) && print -P "%F{yellow}resolvers disagree: normal for CDNs, suspicious otherwise%f"

blocks.text: Append this to the end of the file (in PyCharm or `nano`).
Step 3: Ask the source of truth and test for rewriting

blocks.code:
hr "Authoritative"
ns=$(q $domain NS | head -1)
if [[ -n $ns ]]; then
  auth=$(q @$ns $domain A | sort | paste -sd' ' -)
  print "$ns -> ${auth:-NO ANSWER}"
  dig +noall +answer @$ns $domain A +norecurse | awk 'NR==1 {print "zone TTL:", $2, "s"}'
fi

hr "Rewriting test"
junk=$(q "nx-$RANDOM.invalid")
if [[ -z $junk ]]; then
  print -P "%F{green}OK%f  nonexistent names return nothing"
else
  print -P "%F{red}WARNING%f  a made-up name resolved to: $junk"
fi

blocks.text: Step 4: Run it

Run it against `example.com`, `iana.org` and a domain you own. Compare the resolver lines with the authoritative line. Then change the heading helper into a table or add `+dnssec` to see the `ad` flag.

Make it exit with status 1 when no resolver returns an A record. Add a `-r server` option with `getopts` that adds your own resolver to the comparison, then run it with your router's address to see whether it rewrites anything. Add the SPF and DMARC checks by printing the TXT records at `_dmarc.DOMAIN`.
Try it in the practice terminal

The practice terminal answers `dig`, `nslookup`, `host` and `scutil --dns` for the lab domains with canned data. Run the bulk-resolve loop, ask for MX and NS records, try `dig -x 8.8.8.8 +short`, and compare `dig` with `nslookup` on the same name.
Next
You can find and read the address behind any name. Continue to the next chapter on HTTP and `curl`, where you talk to the server at that address and read its response.

terms.def: A DNS client or server that answers queries; the stub asks, the recursive resolver researches
The minimal DNS client in the operating system that forwards questions to a recursive resolver
A server that finds answers by querying other servers and caches the results
A name server that holds the original records for a zone
The part of the DNS namespace managed together, usually one domain
NS records in a parent zone that hand responsibility for a subdomain to other servers
One DNS entry: name, TTL, class, type and data
DNS status meaning the queried name does not exist
DNS status meaning the resolver could not obtain an answer
A record type making one name an alias of another
Multicast DNS: resolving .local names by asking the local link instead of a server
Sending queries for certain domains to different resolvers, typically a VPN's for internal names
DNS over HTTPS: DNS queries carried inside encrypted HTTPS connections
Signatures on DNS records that let a resolver verify they are genuine
The local /etc/hosts file consulted by the system resolver before DNS
